7. Privacy and Security as System Properties
segments.translation: 7. Confidențialitatea și securitatea ca proprietăți ale sistemului

segments.source: Engineering question: How do we prevent a probabilistic component from becoming a path across trust boundaries?

Security changes the epistemic posture of engineering. Reliability asks what happens when the world differs from our assumptions; security asks what happens when another actor deliberately searches for the assumptions we forgot. Privacy introduces a related constraint: information should not become available merely because a model can infer or reproduce it. Meridian is now connected to confidential repositories and external content. This makes the distinction between untrusted data, model reasoning and privileged action central to the architecture.
7.1 From Training Data to Inference-Time Leakage

A course on privacy across the AI lifecycle should begin with the failure it is meant to prevent, not with the metric that happens to be fashionable. Privacy risk arises during collection, training, fine-tuning, retrieval, logging, prompting and output. Membership inference and training-data extraction show that models can reveal information about their data, while RAG systems introduce direct inference-time paths to sensitive documents. This distinction matters because the same numerical result can support very different conclusions depending on the deployment context. The relevant question is always conditional: what exactly has been observed, under which assumptions, and which future decision is that evidence supposed to justify? Keeping those three parts together prevents a familiar failure of AI projects, in which a technically correct measurement is gradually retold as a much stronger claim than the experiment ever established.

Consider a language assistant that respects document permissions in the source application but indexes text into a shared retrieval store without equivalent access controls. The privacy defect is architectural even if the model itself was never trained on the confidential material. What makes the example useful is the separation between mechanism and symptom. The visible symptom may be an incorrect answer, an unfair alert, an unsafe action or a privacy leak, but the mechanism can sit in the data pipeline, model, retrieval layer, policy engine, user interface or organisational process. A trustworthy-AI investigation therefore resists the urge to repair the first component that looks suspicious. It reconstructs the path that produced the outcome and asks which intervention would actually break that path.

Encryption and access control protect data from unauthorized access, but they do not by themselves constrain what a trained model reveals about individuals whose data influenced training. Differential privacy addresses a different question: how much can the presence or absence of one person's record change the distribution of outputs? DP-SGD made it practical to train deep models with explicit privacy accounting by clipping per-example gradients and adding noise. The price is a trade-off among privacy, utility, model size, and computation.

Differential privacy is valuable precisely because its guarantee is formal and composable, but the guarantee applies to a specified mechanism and privacy budget. It does not automatically protect data copied into prompts, logs, retrieval stores, or tool outputs. Privacy engineering still needs conventional controls around the model.

Carlini and colleagues demonstrated that language models can emit verbatim training examples, including rare sequences, under carefully constructed extraction attacks. Subsequent work has extended membership and reconstruction attacks to pretrained and fine-tuned models. This matters because memorization risk can change across training stages. Fine-tuning, synthetic data, and downstream adaptation can alter which examples are exposed. Privacy evaluation should therefore occur after the actual deployment configuration is built, not only on the base model.

This also changes how evidence is designed. Minimise data, separate purposes, propagate access control into retrieval, redact or tokenize sensitive fields where appropriate, restrict logs and retention, and test extraction scenarios. Use differential privacy when its formal privacy guarantee matches the threat model and utility budget. Evidence should be collected at the level at which a claim can be falsified. Averages are helpful for orientation, but engineers need slices, counterexamples, traces, thresholds and failure cases when those are what determine whether authority should be granted. The most valuable evaluation is often not the one with the most samples; it is the one that can cause the team to change a release decision because it directly exercises an assumption on which the system depends.

A useful discipline is to separate capability evidence from assurance evidence. Capability evidence asks whether the system can perform a task under some conditions. Assurance evidence asks whether it can be relied upon for a specified purpose, which also requires information about failure behavior, detection, containment, human response and change over time. The distinction becomes increasingly important for general-purpose models because impressive competence on difficult benchmarks can coexist with surprisingly simple failures. A trustworthy system needs an account of both sides of that jagged performance profile.

segments.source: 7.2 Adversarial ML, Prompt Injection, and the Supply Chain

A course on AI security should begin with the failure it is meant to prevent, not with the metric that happens to be fashionable. Modern AI combines traditional software vulnerabilities with adversarial manipulation of learned behavior. Evasion, poisoning, model extraction, jailbreaks, indirect prompt injection and compromised model or data dependencies require different threat models. This distinction matters because the same numerical result can support very different conclusions depending on the deployment context. Keeping those three parts together prevents a familiar failure of AI projects, in which a technically correct measurement is gradually retold as a much stronger claim than the experiment ever established.

Consider an agent reading a webpage that contains hidden instructions telling the model to ignore the user and exfiltrate information. The malicious text is data from the application’s perspective but instruction-like content from the model’s perspective, creating a confused-deputy problem. What makes the example useful is the separation between mechanism and symptom. The visible symptom may be an incorrect answer, an unfair alert, an unsafe action or a privacy leak, but the mechanism can sit in the data pipeline, model, retrieval layer, policy engine, user interface or organisational process. A trustworthy-AI investigation therefore resists the urge to repair the first component that looks suspicious. It reconstructs the path that produced the outcome and asks which intervention would actually break that path.

Prompt injection illustrates why LLM security cannot be solved solely by alignment training. A tool-using model processes natural-language instructions from multiple trust domains: the developer, the user, retrieved documents, websites, emails, and tool outputs. If these are concatenated into one context, untrusted content can masquerade as instructions. This is analogous to mixing code and data without a reliable boundary.

Defenses should therefore use architectural separation: typed tool calls, allowlists, least privilege, content provenance, scoped credentials, policy enforcement outside the model, confirmation for high-impact actions, taint tracking where feasible, and monitoring of tool sequences. Natural-language reminders such as 'ignore malicious instructions' can help but should be treated as a soft defense, not a security boundary.

The engineering goal is not to prove the absence of attacks. It is to reduce attack surface, make high-impact actions harder, detect suspicious behavior, contain compromise, and make recovery possible. Security is the trustworthy-AI property most obviously shaped by an intelligent adversary, so the threat model must be expected to evolve.

This also changes how evidence is designed. Map trust boundaries, classify all external content as untrusted, isolate tool credentials, validate tool arguments outside the model, pin and attest dependencies where feasible, test poisoning and injection scenarios, and maintain incident-ready logs. A trustworthy system needs an account of both sides of that jagged performance profile.

7.3 Least Privilege, Provenance, and Defense in Depth

A course on defense-in-depth for AI systems should begin with the failure it is meant to prevent, not with the metric that happens to be fashionable. 8. Verification, Testing, and Evaluation Science
Engineering question: What evidence would genuinely distinguish a dependable AI system from one that merely performs well on familiar tests?

AI evaluation is entering a difficult phase. Benchmarks remain useful, but frontier systems increasingly train on public data, adapt to prompts, use tools and behave differently in realistic environments. The International AI Safety Report 2026 describes an emerging evaluation gap between pre-deployment tests and real-world performance. NIST’s August 2026 draft TEVV-Athlon framework likewise treats test, evaluation, verification and validation as a structured assessment of outcomes across statistical ML, LLMs, multimodal and agentic systems. Meridian’s engineers therefore replace the idea of a single acceptance benchmark with an evidence portfolio.
8.1 A Testing Pyramid for AI Systems

The first useful move is to make AI testing strategy concrete. Tests should exist at the smallest layer where a property can be isolated and at the integrated layer where interactions create new behavior. Dataset checks, component tests, behavioral evaluations, end-to-end scenarios, red teaming and production monitoring answer different questions. This distinction matters because the same numerical result can support very different conclusions depending on the deployment context. The relevant question is always conditional: what exactly has been observed, under which assumptions, and which future decision is that evidence supposed to justify? Keeping those three parts together prevents a familiar failure of AI projects, in which a technically correct measurement is gradually retold as a much stronger claim than the experiment ever established.

Consider a citation validator that can be tested deterministically on known spans, while the full answer-generation pipeline requires scenario tests to discover whether retrieval, generation and formatting interact to create unsupported claims. What makes the example useful is the separation between mechanism and symptom. The visible symptom may be an incorrect answer, an unfair alert, an unsafe action or a privacy leak, but the mechanism can sit in the data pipeline, model, retrieval layer, policy engine, user interface or organisational process. A trustworthy-AI investigation therefore resists the urge to repair the first component that looks suspicious. It reconstructs the path that produced the outcome and asks which intervention would actually break that path.

Formal methods do not remove the specification problem. If we prove that an image classifier does not change its label for any perturbation within a small norm ball, we have proved a precise property. We have not proved that the classifier understands the object, that the perturbation model reflects realistic changes, or that the system will behave safely when its camera fails. Formal verification closes one logical gap while leaving the modeling gap intact.

Testing is broad but incomplete. Verification is complete but narrow. A mature assurance strategy combines them. Formal analysis can protect invariants that are crisp enough to specify, such as access-control constraints, output ranges, safety envelopes, or deterministic policy rules. Stress testing can explore semantic and sociotechnical behaviors that are difficult to formalize, such as manipulation, bias, hallucination, or user overreliance. Monitoring then catches failures that neither pre-deployment method anticipated.

Many important AI failures occur in code that is far easier to verify than the neural network. Data validation, unit conversion, thresholding, access-control checks, routing logic, aggregation, schema transformations, and post-processing can be specified precisely. A trustworthy architecture should exploit this asymmetry. The less critical logic is hidden inside a language model prompt, the more of the system can be subjected to conventional testing, type checking, static analysis, and formal verification.

This also changes how evidence is designed. Build a testing pyramid with fast deterministic checks at the base, statistical behavior tests above them, adversarial and end-to-end scenarios at the system layer, and monitored field performance at the top. Every release should know which claim each test supports. Evidence should be collected at the level at which a claim can be falsified. Averages are helpful for orientation, but engineers need slices, counterexamples, traces, thresholds and failure cases when those are what determine whether authority should be granted. The most valuable evaluation is often not the one with the most samples; it is the one that can cause the team to change a release decision because it directly exercises an assumption on which the system depends.

A useful discipline is to separate capability evidence from assurance evidence. Capability evidence asks whether the system can perform a task under some conditions. Assurance evidence asks whether it can be relied upon for a specified purpose, which also requires information about failure behavior, detection, containment, human response and change over time. The distinction becomes increasingly important for general-purpose models because impressive competence on difficult benchmarks can coexist with surprisingly simple failures. A trustworthy system needs an account of both sides of that jagged performance profile.
segments.translation: O disciplină utilă este separarea dovezilor de capabilitate de dovezile de asigurare. Dovezile de capabilitate întreabă dacă sistemul poate îndeplini o sarcină în anumite condiții. Dovezile de asigurare întreabă dacă ne putem baza pe el pentru un scop specificat, ceea ce necesită și informații despre comportamentul în caz de eșec, detectare, limitarea efectelor, reacția umană și schimbarea în timp. Distincția devine tot mai importantă pentru modelele cu scop general, deoarece competența impresionantă în teste de referință dificile poate coexista cu eșecuri surprinzător de simple. Un sistem demn de încredere are nevoie de o descriere a ambelor laturi ale acestui profil de performanță inegal.

segments.source: The boundary of the claim must remain visible. No test suite covers an open input space. Passing tests can create false confidence when test construction, data provenance or scenario diversity is weak. This is not pedantry. Learned systems are deployed in open environments, and evidence can expire when data, users, models, prompts, tools or incentives change. Good engineering documentation therefore says not only what passed, but what was not tested, what assumptions make the result meaningful, what observations would contradict it and what change would force the evidence to be collected again.

There is also an organisational dimension. A control that exists in a design document but is routinely bypassed is not an effective control; a human approval that receives no useful evidence is not independent oversight; a red-team finding that cannot block a release is not a meaningful safety signal. Trustworthiness becomes real only when measurements are connected to authority. This is why the course repeatedly returns to owners, escalation, rollback, incident review and evidence freshness alongside model metrics.
segments.translation: Există și o dimensiune organizațională. O măsură de control care există într-un document de proiectare, dar este ocolită în mod curent, nu este eficientă; o aprobare umană care nu primește dovezi utile nu reprezintă supraveghere independentă; o constatare red-team care nu poate bloca o lansare nu reprezintă un semnal de siguranță semnificativ. Caracterul demn de încredere devine real numai când măsurările sunt conectate la autoritate. De aceea, cursul revine constant la responsabili, escaladare, revenirea la o versiune anterioară, analiza incidentelor și actualitatea dovezilor, alături de metricile modelului.
